topic: Binary Counting and the Towers of Hanoi: The Logic of Movement
target_audience: High school students or introductory computer science learners

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Language of Binary
sections.content: Briefly introduce binary as a base-2 system using only 0 and 1. Explain that just as decimal (base-10) uses powers of 10, binary uses powers of 2. Use a visual representation of 3 light bulbs (representing 4, 2, and 1) to show how any number can be formed.
sections.example: Visual: 3 bulbs. If the 4-bulb and 1-bulb are ON (101), the value is 5. If all are ON (111), the value is 7.

sections.title: The Towers of Hanoi Challenge
sections.content: Introduce the puzzle: 3 rods and N disks of different sizes. Rules: Only one disk moved at a time; a larger disk cannot sit on a smaller one. Pose the question: What is the minimum number of moves to solve it for 3 disks?
sections.example: Animation: A robotic arm moving disks from Rod A to Rod C, following the rules.

sections.title: Connecting Moves to Binary Counting
sections.content: Reveal the magic link: As you count in binary (1, 2, 3, 4...), the changes in binary digits correspond exactly to disk movements. The bit that changes tells you which disk to move. If the 1st bit changes, move disk 1; if the 2nd bit changes, move disk 2.
sections.example: Table: Count 001 (Move Disk 1), 010 (Move Disk 2), 011 (Move Disk 1), 100 (Move Disk 3).

sections.title: The Power of 2^n - 1
sections.content: Explain why the total moves for 'n' disks is always 2^n - 1. Connect this back to the binary counting limit: a 3-bit binary number can count up to 7 (2^3 - 1).
sections.example: Visual: For 3 disks, 2^3 - 1 = 7 moves. Animation shows the binary counter ticking from 001 to 111 as the disks reach the target rod.

sections.title: Application: The Cosmic Clock
sections.content: Apply the concept to a real-world scale. Mention the Legend of Brahma: 64 golden disks. Calculate the time required to finish (at 1 move per second, it would take over 500 billion years). This highlights the exponential nature of binary growth.
sections.example: Animation: A turtle and a hare. The hare (exponential growth) quickly outpaces the turtle (linear growth) as the number of disks increases.
